extracted.intended_audience: OSHA stakeholders, regulators, employers, occupational safety researchers, and commenters on the Heat Injury and Illness Prevention NPRM
extracted.subtask_description: Rubric and methodological guidance embedded in OSHA's proposed Heat Injury and Illness Prevention standard (NPRM), including literature caveats, distributional analysis methods, industry scope definitions, and technological feasibility assessment procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of exposure-response functions (occupational health literature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposure-response functions used to relate heat exposure to work capacity fall into two groups: (1) empirically-derived functions (e.g., Hothaps, PWC) and (2) guideline-based functions derived from recommended work-rest ratios in NIOSH, ACGIH, ISO guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Hothaps function (Kjellstrom et al., 2014) and PWC function (Foster et al., 2021) are empirically derived; Kjellstrom et al. (2009b), Dunne et al. (2013) reflect guideline-based work-rest recommendations. When selecting or applying an exposure-response function, explicitly state which group it comes from and its original context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveats when borrowing exposure-response functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirically-derived exposure-response functions are context-specific, and guideline-based functions were designed to reduce illness rather than to estimate causal effects on work capacity. Applying these functions to different populations assumes the average worker conforms to the source population's behavior or to guideline-recommended work-rest ratios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about external validity: e.g., Hothaps is based on acclimatized outdoor workers in hotter regions; PWC is based on unacclimatized young adults in indoor chambers. Studies using guideline-based functions may overestimate economic costs because guidelines aim to prevent illness, not measure productivity loss. Document assumptions and limitations when applying functions to other worker populations or macroeconomic models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of payroll/output changes (demand and cost confounding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed associations between heat and non-agricultural economic output (e.g., payroll) may reflect demand-side effects or increased firm costs in addition to changes in labor productivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using payroll or output measures as proxies for productivity, consider alternative explanations (reduced demand for goods/services, increased firm costs such as higher AC usage) and discuss potential spillover from agricultural yield reductions. Adjust analyses or caveat conclusions accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worker utility as an effect of heat exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat exposure not only affects productivity and supply but also reduces worker utility — causes discomfort, makes work more arduous, and can have social and leisure impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use surveys and qualitative evidence to capture disutility (e.g., time/resources coping with heat, exhaustion affecting family life, longer shifts to avoid hot periods). Consider reported intentions to change jobs and market-power issues (e.g., monopsony) when assessing welfare impacts beyond wages and productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize labor productivity and labor supply as distinct channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat exposure can decrease labor productivity (effort/output per hour) and/or reduce labor supply (attendance, hours worked), and can impact mental performance and broader economic output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate effects in empirical work and policy analysis: quantify both productivity-per-hour changes and changes in hours/attendance; link channel identification to chosen exposure-response functions and to worker/firm incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for workplace incentive structures when estimating productivity effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Workplace factors—wage structure (piece-rate, hourly, salary), management techniques, mechanization, and supervisor monitoring—affect how workers adjust effort under heat and therefore affect estimated productivity impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly model or stratify by pay structure and monitoring. Evidence: piece-rate can induce compensatory effort (blunting observed productivity declines) but may have health/safety consequences; physiological constraints can limit effort increases at high temperatures; fixed-wage-but-monitored workers may shift effort from quality to quantity. Discuss interactions with minimum wage laws where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess availability and effects of adaptation measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Adaptation measures (engineering controls such as climate control/air-conditioning, lighting that reduces heat, and acclimatization protocols) can mitigate negative labor productivity effects of heat exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate presence/coverage of engineering controls at workplace level (e.g., factory A/C, LED lighting). Consider evidence that controls can eliminate productivity declines but not necessarily labor-supply reductions. Consider mixed evidence on acclimatization effectiveness (short-term vs long-term acclimatization, sport vs occupational contexts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of American Community Survey (ACS) data for distributional analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Distributional analysis uses ACS microdata (2018–2022) for worker-level demographic and economic characteristics to quantify fractions of workers benefiting from the standard across groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include only employed workers aged 16+. Record and process variables: age (10-year bins, 65+ top bin); race/ethnicity groups (Hispanic, Black, Asian incl. Pacific Islander, White non-Hispanic, other); sex; total family income converted to deciles; disability presence collapsed to single indicator for any disability; U.S. citizenship; infer LGBTQ+ status from co-resident same-sex partner. Document processing choices and years used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merging ACS with exposure measures (aggregation and weighting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Merge ACS worker records with exposure fractions calculated by industry and occupation. Exposure originally calculated at 4-digit NAICS and detailed (6-digit) SOC codes; aggregated to 2-digit NAICS by 4-digit SOC for consistency with ACS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregate by computing weighted-average fraction of workers exposed (separately for outdoor and indoor/process-heat/inadequate_climate_control exposures) in each industry-occupation pair. Use number of workers in each 4-digit NAICS by 6-digit SOC category as weights. Clearly state aggregation levels and weighting scheme in methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculate exposure shares by demographic/economic groups using person-weights
rubrics_metrics.description: For each heterogeneity dimension (age, race/ethnicity, income decile, disability, sex, citizenship, LGBTQ+ proxy), calculate the average share of exposed workers weighted by ACS person-weights to produce representative national estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report results visually (e.g., percent exposed on y-axis vs income deciles on x-axis) and in tables. Explicitly document weighting and how exposure fractions from industry-occupation merges were applied to ACS records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define scope of in-scope core and non-core industries using NAICS codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify industries in-scope for the cost analysis by enumerating relevant 4-digit NAICS codes for core industry categories (e.g., Agriculture; Building Materials; Construction; Manufacturing; Transportation; Utilities; etc.) and a separate list of non-core industries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide full lists (as in Table VIII.K.1 and Table VIII.K.2) of included 4-digit NAICS codes for core and non-core categories so that affected-worker counts and cost calculations are reproducible. Use consistent NAICS vintages and document mapping decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological feasibility legal standard (case-law definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA must show, by substantial evidence, that standards are technologically feasible: protective measures required already exist, can be brought into existence with available technology, or can be created with technology reasonably expected to be developed (per case law cited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite relevant cases (American Textile Mfrs. Inst. v. Donovan (Cotton Dust), United Steelworkers v. Marshall (Lead I), Am. Iron & Steel Inst. v. OSHA (Lead II)). For each provision, describe how required measures meet the technological feasibility threshold and provide evidence (examples of existing controls, industry practices, or plausible near-term development).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology for technological feasibility analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate each proposed provision to identify requirements that imply engineering controls or facility/equipment changes versus those establishing programs/processes/procedures; review current workplace control practices and recommended practices from trade associations and standards organizations; group establishments by exposure source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group establishments into indoor settings (distinguish equipment/process-generated heat vs ambient heat) and outdoor settings (including mobile/transient sites). For provisions requiring engineering controls, demonstrate existing implementation or practicable pathways. Document review of industry practices and guidance from standards bodies as evidence of feasibility.
